Aug. 31: Monday's news to know
By Todd Zola

A dozen evening affairs comprise a relatively busy Monday docket, beginning at 6:05 p.m. ET with the San Francisco Giants visiting the Atlanta Braves. Overall this month, scoring has been trending down. However, early weather forecasts portend a high-scoring slate to close out play for August. Rain may be an issue, however, when the Colorado Rockies host the Baltimore Orioles at 8:40 p.m. ET.

Elly De La Cruz left yesterday's contest in the seventh inning with a tight left quad. After the game, Cincinnati Reds manager Terry Francona indicated the team didn't believe the injury was serious, suggesting the star shortstop could return to the lineup tonight for the opener of a home series with the San Diego Padres.
The Seattle Mariners are set to call up Lazaro Montes, the club's No. 4 prospect on Kiley McDaniel's updated 2026 top 10 prospect rankings for all 30 MLB teams. The 21-year-old outfielder began the season with Double-A Arkansas, posting a .234/.369/.550 line over 79 games. He has spent the last 43 games with Triple-A Tacoma, batting .267/.359/.564. Power is Montes' forte, but he must cut down on the over 30% strikeout rate he recorded at both minor league levels. He'll likely play right field, shifting Dominic Canzone to DH.
The Minnesota Twins finally placed Byron Buxton on the 10-day IL for his lingering hip issue. He missed four consecutive games prior to the move. Walker Jenkins has been handling center field and should play regularly while Buxton is out, which could be the rest of the season. Earlier in the year, it was reported that Buxton needs surgery on his hip. Instead of waiting for the offseason, he could be shut down soon and then go under the knife.
The St. Louis Cardinals will be without NL Rookie of the Year candidate JJ Wetherholt for at least 10-days after placing him on the IL due to right wrist tendinitis. Struggles over the past month have dropped him behind Sal Stewart in the race for freshman honors. Missing time may make it hard for him to make up ground with voters.

Be sure to check out the latest fantasy lineup advice as well as the MLB betting tips for Monday.

Aug. 30: Sunday morning's news to know

By Todd Zola

Today's schedule gets an early 12:15 p.m. ET start with the Washington Nationals entertaining the Miami Marlins. Thirteen matinees follow, with the fantasy period ending with the Cincinnati Reds visiting the Chicago Cubs at 7:20 p.m. ET. Due to a scheduling quirk, the Arizona Diamondbacks and San Francisco Giants have a rare Sunday off.

After several false alarms, Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy indicated that Roman Anthony and Trevor Story are expected to be activated from the IL and join the club for the finale of a four-game series in the Bronx against the New York Yankees. Anthony's pathway to playing time is clearer, as he'll take over primary DH duties. Story will need to vie for action with Andruw Monasterio, Nick Sogard and Anthony Seigler.
The Yankees reported that the initial diagnosis of George Lombard Jr.'s knee injury is encouraging. The rookie shortstop hurt his knee on a swing during the second game of yesterday's doubleheader. Lombard's status will be updated after they finish evaluating his imaging. If Lombard is forced to miss action, Jose Caballero is the likely replacement.
The New York Mets reinstated Juan Soto from the 10-day IL prior to yesterday's game with the Houston Astros. He was sidelined for almost a month with a Grade 2 calf strain. Soto opted to skip a rehab assignment, but he still went 1-for-4 with a run and RBI in his return. The club cleared a roster spot by placing Luis Roberts on waivers. The veteran outfielder has been productive in August, but he's likely to clear waivers and potentially return to the Mets' active roster.
The Los Angeles Dodgers were hopeful that Shohei Ohtani would start today's road tilt with the Detroit Tigers. They expected only an inning or two, but after the two-way phenom cut short Friday's bullpen session, his return to the hill was delayed indefinitely. Tyler Glasnow is moving up a day to face the Tigers.

stories.headline: Inside Brendan Sorsby's eligibility saga and the scars it left
stories.summary: The fighting behind the scenes between the Big 12 and Texas Tech, and the NFL's ultimate decision of denial.
stories.byline: Max Olson, Heather Dinich, Jeremy Fowler, David Purdum
stories.body:
EDITOR'S NOTE: This story originally ran on July 7, 2026. It has been updated ahead of Week 1 of the 2026 season.

FOUR PIECES OF paper from a district courthouse in West Texas were all it took to set the college football world ablaze.

The gambling addiction that quarterback Brendan Sorsby privately dealt with throughout his four years in college, while impermissibly wagering at least $90,000, had finally come to light in April. The NCAA uncovered Sorsby's violation of one of its most fundamental rules in placing thousands of bets on college and professional sports during his time at Indiana, Cincinnati and now Texas Tech.

While Sorsby was away for a 35-day treatment program in Arizona, Texas Tech's administration worked through the standard NCAA processes for reinstatement from permanent ineligibility. Based on the rulebook and recent precedent, the severity of Sorsby's violations, including 40 bets placed on Indiana football as a freshman in 2022, would be practically impossible to overcome.

So Sorsby's legal team attempted what many viewed as a Hail Mary, suing the NCAA in district court May 18 in the hopes an injunction could buy him enough time to chase a College Football Playoff national championship with the Red Raiders this fall.

And when it actually worked, as so many courtroom challenges of the NCAA have in recent years, with a retired Texas judge signing off on a four-page temporary injunction on the morning of June 8, that's when the real battles began.

"For whatever reason," Ron Slavin, Sorsby's agent, said, "the world melted down like college football was ruined forever."

The two-month drama over Sorsby's eligibility triggered a series of disputes: Texas Tech vs. the NCAA, Sorsby vs. the NCAA, the Big 12 vs. Texas Tech and eventually Sorsby vs. the NFL. Emotions within the Big 12 were high, and sources told ESPN that the league athletic directors wanted to hold Texas Tech accountable in some way if the school ultimately played Sorsby. It was a fight over critical moral, ethical and legal issues, as the Big 12 later described it in a court filing, and it came with a significant toll.

As Texas Tech readies for the 2026 season, its reputation as a football program and institution has taken an undeniable hit. The Big 12's relationship with its new powerhouse has, too. NCAA president Charlie Baker called the district court loss "a new low" for these turbulent times. The incident further exposed the NCAA's inability to enforce its own rules but also showed a blueprint for how a conference might legally flex when needed. Sorsby is out millions of dollars, and his playing career is on hold. There were few winners to be found by the end of this affair.

ESPN pieced together the inside story of how the Sorsby saga threatened to start a war within a conference, and the public posturing, private phone calls and surprise lawsuits that ultimately blocked the prized QB from playing and kept the peace ... for now. ESPN spoke to multiple sources, including Big 12 athletic directors, university presidents and chancellors, NCAA staff, and sources at Texas Tech. Sorsby could not be reached for comment.

Now that it's finally over, Texas Tech officials said they don't believe they did anything wrong. Cody Campbell, their billionaire board chair, said this is one of those moments that people don't forgive and forget.

"This thing was not tried in court," Campbell said. "I mean, it was. But it was tried in the court of public opinion."

JUDGE KEN CURRY surprised almost everyone when he granted Sorsby's temporary injunction June 8. Multiple Texas Tech sources told ESPN they were preparing for that outcome but weren't expecting it.

One official who sat in Lubbock County Court a week earlier believed Sorsby had a chance after witnessing what he described as a "superstar" performance from Jeffrey Kessler, Sorsby's lead attorney, in making his case against the NCAA over the course of a two-hour hearing.

"He's the Harlem Globetrotters. He doesn't lose," Slavin later said of Kessler. "And the NCAA, unfortunately, is the Washington Generals."

Curry, a retired judge from Fort Worth, granted an injunction but offered little rationale for his decision. Mark Hicks, the NCAA's managing director of enforcement, called the ruling "disappointing" from an integrity standpoint.

"Betting on your own games, betting on your own teams is a line that we had been clear that we just, even as a membership in national office, we're just not going to cross," Hicks said. "And it felt undermining to have that rule and everything behind that rule stripped away pretty quickly with a state court judge."

Curry's ruling called for Sorsby to serve a two-game suspension -- a punishment Sorsby's legal team had initially offered to the NCAA as a concession -- and to continue treatment for his diagnosed gambling and anxiety disorders. Texas Tech installed apps on the quarterback's devices to block any future betting and put a plan in place for his continued recovery.

Outrage was expected and arrived immediately. Kansas State athletic director Gene Taylor called the injunction "f---ing bulls---." His peers in the Big 12 were just as stunned and offended. Georgia AD Josh Brooks and Nebraska AD Troy Dannen informed their coaching staffs they were not allowed to schedule games against Texas Tech. Michigan canceled a volleyball match scheduled for September, while the rest of the Big Ten considered taking a similar stand.

"It wasn't about the kid," Taylor told ESPN. "It was about the issue. That's the one thing we all know you can't do in this business."

Texas Tech had stuck to a careful public relations strategy up to that point, focusing its message on extending its full support to Sorsby. When the NCAA officially rejected his request for reinstatement in late May and the school chose to appeal, Texas Tech president Lawrence Schovanec penned a 900-word letter to the campus community explaining the school's rationale.

"Brendan himself has been open about his struggle with severe gambling addiction," Schovanec wrote, "and we believe his vulnerability deserves to be met with the full weight of this institution's support."

The intense criticism of Texas Tech throughout college athletics got noisy enough that Texas Tech officials sat down the day after the injunction was granted to record a message to Red Raiders supporters that laid out all the facts. When they were done filming, school officials agreed the segment came across as too scripted, according to sources briefed on the discussions. They scrapped that plan.

But the anonymous quotes from rivals and other schools talking of boycotting Texas Tech offended Campbell, whose wealth and position as the chair of the school's board of regents have made him a powerful but polarizing figure throughout college athletics. In an interview with Dan Dakich on June 10, Campbell fired back at the detractors, telling them, "Don't hate the player, hate the game."

"If this had happened at LSU, people would say, 'Ah, it's LSU,'" Campbell said. "They're always going to do what they do. But it happened at Texas Tech, and people don't want to compete with us."

That same day, amid what sources described as mounting pressure from Texas Tech's office of the chancellor, school leadership agreed to re-record the message. Athletic director Kirby Hocutt, Schovanec, coach Joey McGuire, and senior associate ADs Grant Stovall and Robert Giovanetti reconvened for their second attempt. The final cut was 21 minutes long and published on the night of June 11.

The group cared only about their message getting to Texas Tech fans, and the initial feedback from their target audience was positive. But once rival fanbases found it and derided it, the video got nearly 6 million views on X.

This was Texas Tech's impossible challenge following the injunction: There were no magic words that could make everyone OK with Sorsby playing this season.

The criticism of the 21-minute video was negative enough, not just from the public but also from some Texas Tech stakeholders, that sources said Schovanec had second thoughts the next day about whether Texas Tech could stay the course.

Texas Tech's athletic council called a Sunday meeting on June 14 at Jones AT&T Stadium. Campbell and fellow regents Dusty Womble, Clay Cash and Tim Culp sat down with Schovanec, Hocutt, McGuire and Texas Tech's general counsel. Sorsby joined the group for a portion of the three-hour session, Campbell told ESPN.

The topic: How much further was Texas Tech willing to go? Campbell and others were motivated to keep fighting. Others were feeling more apprehensive as they talked through strategy. The greatest fear at that time, according to multiple people who attended the meeting, was of the uncertainties beyond their control.

If continuing to back Sorsby and playing him in games could potentially result in the Red Raiders being deemed ineligible for the Big 12 championship game and the College Football Playoff, Campbell said all parties -- including Sorsby -- agreed that would be too unfair of a burden for the other 106 players in the program.

During that Sunday meeting in Lubbock, Schovanec stepped out to take a phone call from Big 12 commissioner Brett Yormark. Two sources told ESPN that Yormark asked to set up a meeting with the Big 12 presidents in the hopes of working things out before the situation escalated any further.

Meanwhile, Yormark was convening his own private meetings with the rest of his Big 12 members and preparing what would be a course-altering legal maneuver.

THE NEWS OF Sorsby's temporary injunction broke a little after 7 a.m. in Las Vegas as college athletic directors gathered at the Mandalay Bay Resort for the annual National Association of Collegiate Directors of Athletics conference. A handful of Big 12 athletic directors huddled soon after.

"We were just beside ourselves," one AD told ESPN. "Like, how can this happen?"

In the first conference call between Big 12 athletic directors the following day, Hocutt participated and, sources said, four ADs -- Kansas State's Taylor, TCU's Mike Buddie, Iowa State's Jamie Pollard and Utah's Mark Harlan -- were most outspoken on the subject.

"I would say it was cordial but very direct," a source on the call said. "Like, this is wrong on a lot of levels."

Hocutt repeated what he had stated publicly, expressing the school's desire to continue supporting Sorsby. His colleagues on the call pushed back, reminding him Iowa State had not fought this in 2023 when quarterback Hunter Dekkers and several other starters lost their eligibility over sports wagering. They argued that Texas Tech could continue to support Sorsby and his recovery without playing the quarterback.

"You can shut this down right away," one person said.

According to a source, the Big Ten did not have formal talks about boycotting Texas Tech from its athletics schedules but did discuss the issue on a weekly call with athletic directors.

"It kind of felt like it was a low point in a way," one Big Ten AD said. "Just very frustrated. I don't know if I've ever seen a more emotional response to anything. It almost felt like, gosh, now we lose that, it's like, can you have rules around anything? If you can't have a rule on that, then what are we doing?"

Yormark took a measured approach internally with his initial response, sources said, encouraging his athletic directors to "take a step back" on their first call and not overreact while the conference worked with its legal counsel to determine potential options.

Following the call, Big 12 ADs privately discussed what steps the conference ought to take. While Buddie told ESPN he anticipated Big 12 schools would have conversations about refusing to play Texas Tech this season, those talks never went far.

"I don't know how serious that was," a Big 12 AD said. "I think people knew that was a bit of a stretch. But I think we were very serious that if Brendan played in games, those games should not count towards the conference championship and we should hold them out of the conference championship. At a minimum, if he played, they were going to forfeit those games and they couldn't qualify for the Big 12 championship.

"I think it was very clear, 15-1, that we were going to do something as a conference, or needed to do something as a conference."

But could the Big 12 take preemptive action against Texas Tech when Sorsby hadn't played in a game with his new team? The conference received a letter from Texas attorney general Ken Paxton on June 11, warning that sanctioning Texas Tech for complying with the court order would be unlawful and expose the Big 12 to "substantial liability" for antitrust issues, breach of contract and tortious interference. Paxton, who is running for U.S. Senate, wrote that the total exposure for the conference and its members would be "substantially more than $200 million."

The Oklahoma, Kansas and Utah attorneys general responded within 24 hours, publicly rejecting Paxton's threats and backing the Big 12's right to sanction its members. Oklahoma AG Gentner Drummond called on the Big 12 to suspend Sorsby, decrying Texas Tech's actions as a "shameful chapter in the story of college football."

By Friday, the Big 12 was discussing taking this matter to federal court with the league's outside counsel, Sidley Austin. Its league bylaws permit the conference to sanction members who engage in actions "materially averse to the best interests" of the Big 12, including restrictions on revenue distributions and postseason bans. But was Yormark willing to take it that far?

"Throughout, it was like, 'Hey guys, this is really a family dispute, but it's a family dispute with national consequences,'" a Big 12 source said. "[Yormark] was trying to figure out how to leave Texas Tech some outs, how to create some alternative pathways for them. He didn't want to blow the conference up over this."

Yormark called what a Big 12 AD described as an "emergency meeting" Sunday night with Big 12 presidents, chancellors and general counsel, excluding Schovanec, and explained the federal lawsuit the conference would bring against Texas Tech and Paxton in the Northern District of Texas. The board supported the maneuver, and the 47-page suit was filed around midnight CT.

"It was a left hook," one Big 12 AD said, "that I don't think anybody saw coming."

The lawsuit sought declaratory judgments and injunctive relief affirming the Big 12's authority to enforce its bylaws and sanction Texas Tech if Sorsby played in any conference games. On that same Monday, the NCAA filed its appeal in Lubbock County District Court seeking an expedited resolution by Aug. 28, one day before the start of the college football season.

Campbell said Texas Tech leaders met once again Monday and arrived at the conclusion that, even if they believed they were on solid legal ground, there was no way to resolve these cases and guarantee Sorsby's eligibility before his June 22 deadline to apply for the NFL's supplemental draft.

"There was no way for Brendan to do what was right for Brendan, and it was going to be hanging over the team's heads all summer and maybe into the season," Campbell said. "We just couldn't do that."

That Monday night, Campbell posted a three-page letter announcing Sorsby's departure and McGuire called a 7:45 p.m. team meeting to inform his players they would move forward without him.

After an intense week, one Big 12 athletic director described the sudden resolution as "a little bit anticlimactic." The Big 12 was just grateful the ordeal was over.

"Collectively, there was a big sigh of relief," a Big 12 source said.

SORSBY AND HIS camp believed all along that they had the exit ramp of the NFL supplemental draft as a potential option. His reps contacted the league in early May to inquire about applying and were told the deadline was June 22.

The quarterback contemplated entering the draft last December, according to Slavin, and the agent preferred that option over entering the transfer portal. On New Year's Eve, an NFL general manager contacted Slavin asking whether Sorsby was serious about staying in school. One AFC executive told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler that Sorsby would've been a late first-round pick. But after another winless run through November with the Bearcats, Sorsby wanted to compete for the Heisman Trophy and chase a national championship as a senior.

In the days after Texas Tech parted ways with Sorsby, his legal team dropped its lawsuit against the NCAA and applied for the supplemental draft. A source familiar with the situation said Texas Tech's coaching staff talked with roughly 65-70 NFL personnel people who sought more information on Sorsby, and they were working to get Red Raiders receivers cleared to catch passes for him at a July pro day in Dallas.

Slavin attempted to make the case for Sorsby in several public interviews, framing the bets the quarterback placed on Indiana football as mistakes made by an 18-year-old and emphasizing that he never bet on games he played in.

That argument might've been good enough for a judge in Texas, but the NFL wasn't convinced. One day after the deadline passed, the NFL sent a scathing letter informing Sorsby it would not accommodate him and hold a supplemental draft.

A player hasn't been selected in a supplemental draft since 2019, and the NFL wasn't compelled to grant Sorsby that privilege. The letter penned by Larry Ferazani, general counsel for the NFL's management council, said Sorsby's issues were too significant and "too closely tied to the League's core integrity interests" to be meaningfully reviewed in just a few days.

Ferazani's letter offered perhaps the harshest assessment of Sorsby's actions to date, calling out his repeated NCAA violations at three universities, his efforts to avoid detection by funding others betting on his behalf and the possibility he violated state criminal law.

"Your Petition does not address these matters," Ferazani wrote. "Nor does it demonstrate accountability for your conduct or indicate whether, or how, you would adhere to the League's rules and policies governing the integrity of competition. Instead, even after receiving notice of the NCAA's decision rescinding your college eligibility in May, you sought to avoid the consequences of that determination through litigation rather than accepting responsibility for your actions, and you pursued entry into the NFL only after abandoning those efforts."

The NFL's management council spent significant time reviewing Sorsby's case once the application was sent. A source with direct knowledge of the NFL's process described it as a "very comprehensive review." Commissioner Roger Goodell trusted the council with the process, the source said, adding that the league was confident in its position.

Among the many concerns the council identified: Sorsby's gambling history over four years, the short notice of requesting the supplemental draft and what the league felt was a flimsy case made by Sorsby's team.

"No defense, no supporting documents -- nothing came in," the source said. "[The NFL] didn't have the ability to look at what took place."

The league could've considered accepting Sorsby's application for a supplemental draft and then given him a suspension during his rookie season, much as it did with a five-game suspension for former Ohio State quarterback Terrelle Pryor in 2011 following his supplemental selection, matching the NCAA sanctions he was avoiding. But, per the source, the league never got to that point.

One AFC executive told ESPN he was somewhat surprised Sorsby's application was denied because his gambling preceded his dealings with the league. They wondered whether what they perceived as a lack of contrition from Sorsby was a factor.

"I think he underestimated the reaction," the executive said. "He should have been begging to get accepted."

Kessler called the rejection "a violation of the CBA and the law" and said he would immediately pursue the issue with the NFL Players Association. Others were skeptical the NFLPA would challenge the league's decision because Sorsby is not yet a member of the union. As the league source put it, "You'd essentially be taking a job from a union member."

The NFL informed teams in a memo last week that Sorsby has decided not to pursue litigation and will be eligible for the 2027 draft. He won't face discipline from the NFL for his past betting, but an NFL source told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that the league is reserving the right to investigate his conduct and would factor it into discipline for any future violations.

After backing Sorsby as long as he did, Campbell said the news of the NFL's rejection was tough to take.

"We expected that he would be taken in the supplemental draft. Well, that didn't happen," he said. "That just compounds my kind of guilt around this. Should we have just faced the fire? But, man, it took a toll on everybody."

THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Texas Tech and the Big 12 has been tumultuous over the past two years.

It began in 2024 with drama around headset communications. Texas Tech asked the Big 12 to investigate its losses to TCU and Baylor to ensure the integrity of the games was not compromised amid concerns its opponents could've accessed unencrypted coach-to-player communication. Within 24 hours, the Big 12 announced it had conducted a review and had found no concerns.

The Big 12 banned Texas Tech's fan tradition of throwing tortillas onto the field ahead of the 2025 season, then handed down a $25,000 fine after multiple violations during the school's win over Kansas. Jayhawks coach Lance Leipold alleged that a knife was thrown at his team's sideline during the game, then rescinded that claim days later.

In late March, Campbell protested the Big 12 and Fox moving Texas Tech's conference opener against Houston to a Friday night kickoff, calling the decision "absolutely absurd." Yormark responded in an interview with the Lubbock Avalanche-Journal.

"Cody Campbell does not run the Big 12," Yormark said.

But Campbell and Texas Tech did give the Big 12 a true title contender last season with the Red Raiders' dominant run to their first Big 12 championship and the No. 4 seed in the College Football Playoff.

The conference needs nationally relevant programs more than ever since Oklahoma and Texas departed for the SEC. No other conference member is investing in athletics and talent acquisition to the extent Texas Tech is right now. And even without Sorsby, the Red Raiders remain the clear favorites to win the Big 12 again this fall.

Texas Tech's leaders have been key allies for Yormark since his hiring in 2022. Schovanec was chairman of the Big 12 board of directors during Yormark's first year on the job as he negotiated a media rights extension and aggressively pursued conference expansion, and Hocutt quickly became a trusted confidant.

As Big 12 media days kick off Tuesday in Frisco, Texas, and the conference shifts its attention past the events of these past two months, there's work to be done in mending the relationship between conference and school. Some Texas Tech sources insisted they'll be fine and move forward. But ask Campbell where things stand with the Big 12 and it's clear some frustrations still linger.

"I feel like they did not handle this particular situation well, but I have some confidence they're going to be better in the future," Campbell said. "Look, if you have a disagreement in your family, you need to handle things as a family internally. You don't need to air it out publicly. I think that's what we're looking for in the future."

Yormark can argue that, given the undisputed facts of Sorsby's case, this particular issue would've been a 15-1 vote for conference members no matter the player or school. If Sorsby were still at Cincinnati this spring, would Texas Tech have supported his cause? After going through it, though, it's not easy for Campbell and others to step back and see it that way.

McGuire preaches to his players about having a "what's next" mentality. That favorite mantra will come in handy in the months ahead.

Campbell is still pushing for long-term reform and has been closely involved with the Protect College Sports Act as a member of the President's Council on Sports, Fitness and Nutrition as well as lobbying efforts on Capitol Hill. Texas Tech officials hope the Sorsby saga can spur real conversation on how these cases are handled and penalized after learning just how pervasive sports wagering has become.

Last year, an NCAA amendment passed that would have removed penalties for student-athletes who bet on pro sports before membership -- including Texas Tech -- voted to rescind the measure late in the process. Still, the potential of the NCAA relaxing its rules on sports betting drew concern from Congress.

Hicks, a 20-year NCAA veteran, said he couldn't recall anything like what played out over the six days after the injunction was granted.

"I think one big question that college sports has is, do we want to be governed?" Hicks said. "What you saw was a membership that really became vocal and in opposition and well beyond just what we do here at the national office. And I thought that was particularly telling. Now, whether that means that long term they want to be governed, I don't know."

What's next for Sorsby? For now, he's living in Dallas and intends to continue his training and counseling there. Texas Tech officials said he's still welcome in their facilities, and they remain committed to providing him the resources and support he needs to continue his recovery process.

No matter how anybody else felt about it, they hope they sent a message that Texas Tech will always stand behind its student-athletes.

On Saturday, the Red Raiders will take the field without Sorsby. It's a squad that, at least on paper, still looks too loaded to fail. Texas Tech is the Big 12's best candidate to make a deep College Football Playoff run. And if all goes according to plan, Yormark will be standing on a stage in AT&T Stadium in December, handing the defending champs their trophy.

In the meantime, can this uneasy truce endure?

"These things leave scars," one Texas Tech source said.

stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Warriors offseason recap/season preview

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Suns offseason recap/season preview

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28
Key additions: G Darius Acuff Jr., F Alex Karaban, G Emanuel Sharp

Key subtractions: G DeMar DeRozan, G Russell Westbrook

Key retentions: F Precious Achiuwa

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Of those four, Murray appears the most locked-in as a stable member of the team's long-term vision. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Kings offseason recap/season preview

Northwest Division

Portland Trail Blazers: Aug. 17
Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Key retentions: C Robert Williams III

Key subtractions: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, G Matisse Thybulle

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. New owner Tom Dundon's aggressive cost-cutting measures and ongoing fight for arena financing have distracted from the progress that Portland made on the court last season, when it reached the playoffs for the first time since 2021.

Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Blazers offseason recap/season preview

Utah Jazz: Aug. 18
Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Key retentions: C Jusuf Nurkic

Key subtractions: C Walker Kessler

The Jazz finally got some lottery luck, landing at No. 2 and taking Peterson, a gifted guard who has the potential to emerge as the face of the franchise. The hope was that Peterson would be the final major piece in Utah's rebuild, but that plan featured Kessler as the team's long-term starting center. Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Jazz offseason recap/season preview

Minnesota Timberwolves: Aug. 19
Key additions: G LaMelo Ball, G Josh Green, G Isaiah Evans

Key subtractions: F Julius Randle, C Naz Reid

Key retentions: G Ayo Dosunmu, G Bones Hyland, G Jaylen Clark

Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly continued to show his aggression, orchestrating a four-team trade with the Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets that sent out three-time All-Star Randle and the 2023-24 Sixth Man of the Year, Reid, and a future first-round pick to bring in the talented -- but polarizing -- Ball.

That move followed Connelly inking 6-foot-4 guard Dosunmu to a five-year, $112 million extension in June, following his acquisition at the deadline.

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

Coach Chris Finch also lost his top lieutenant on the bench, Micah Nori, who left to coach the Portland Trail Blazers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Timberwolves offseason recap/season preview

Oklahoma City Thunder: Aug. 20
Key additions: C Aday Mara, G Bennett Stirtz

Key retentions: G Kenrich Williams, C Isaiah Hartenstein

Key subtractions: G Isaiah Joe, G Aaron Wiggins, G Luguentz Dort

The extensions for both Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren triggered in July, leading to a trio of financially motivated trades to slash the tax bill and cost-control the current roster.

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

That would mean extra breathing room to eventually extend core young players such as Cason Wallace and Ajay Mitchell. Wallace, the likely replacement starter for Dort, is extension eligible off his rookie contract into October. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Thunder offseason recap/season preview

Denver Nuggets: Aug. 21
Key additions: Marvin Bagley III, Lonnie Walker IV

Key retentions: Spencer Jones, Tyus Jones

Key subtractions: Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas

Finding a resolution to Watson's restricted free agency was Denver's most important piece of summer business.

Watson is a draft success story, rising from the 30th overall pick into one of the league's more intriguing young two-way wings. But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

After Wednesday's deal to send Watson to Cleveland, Denver's front office can shift its attention to escaping the salary cap's second apron. The Nuggets are currently the league's only team above it. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Nuggets offseason recap/season preview

Southwest Division

Memphis Grizzlies: Aug. 14
Key additions: F Cameron Boozer, G D'Angelo Russell, F Isaiah Stewart, F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, C Quinten Post

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: G Ja Morant, F Santi Aldama

Memphis finally traded Ja Morant, turning the last page from an ultimately disappointing chapter in franchise history, and already has his replacement as the face of the franchise in place: No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer. GM Zach Kleiman has overhauled the roster in the past few transaction cycles, acquiring four first-round picks when he traded Desmond Bane, a few more when he dealt Jaren Jackson Jr. and none for Morant, whose departure signaled a fresh start for the Grizzlies and him.

Memphis is in a full-blown youth movement, as 21-year-old forward GG Jackson is now the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Grizzlies say they believe they have a long-term foundation in place with their last few lottery picks: center Zach Edey, small forward Cedric Coward and power forward Boozer. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Grizzlies offseason recap/season preview

New Orleans Pelicans: Aug. 13
Key additions: None

Key retentions: C DeAndre Jordan

Key subtractions: F Kevon Looney

Despite capturing a combined 47 wins over the last two seasons under executive vice president Joe Dumars and general manager Troy Weaver, the Pelicans clearly believe that internal growth is the best path forward. Perhaps that justifies a near-silent summer in which the hiring of new coach Jamahl Mosley turned out to be the team's most notable move. Mosley becomes New Orleans' third coach since Dumars took the helm in April 2025. In addition to drafting Jaron Pierre Jr. in the second round, New Orleans signed just two new players over the summer in Kobe Bufkin and Hunter Dickinson, while bringing back 14 of the 15 players from last season's squad. -- Michael C. Wright

Read the full Pelicans offseason recap/season preview

Dallas Mavericks: Aug. 12
Key additions: F Morez Johnson Jr., F Zaccharie Risacher

Key retentions: Moussa Cisse

Key subtractions: Khris Middleton, Ryan Nembhard

The major changes made by the Mavericks this offseason were in the managerial and coaching ranks. After a seasonlong search, team governor Patrick Dumont hired Masai Ujiri to run the franchise's basketball operations, bringing the architect of the Toronto Raptors' 2019 title team to Dallas. Ujiri decided to part ways with coach Jason Kidd and recruited Dusty May, fresh off an NCAA title with Michigan, to replace him.

Johnson, who played for May at Michigan before the Mavs selected him with the No. 9 pick in the draft, is the headliner of the additions to the roster. Dallas added three potential immediate contributors in a six-team deal, acquiring former Grizzlies forward Santi Aldama, ex-Pistons guard Marcus Sasser and EuroLeague veteran Tarik Biberovic. The franchise also landed former No. 1 pick as part of the trade that sent Luguentz Dort from the Oklahoma City Thunder to the Atlanta Hawks. -- MacMahon

Read the full Mavericks offseason recap/season preview

Houston Rockets: Aug. 11
Key additions: G Marcus Smart, G Bogdan Bogdanovic

Key retentions: F Tari Eason

Key subtractions: F Dorian Finney-Smith, G Josh Okogie

After suffering a first-round postseason exit for the second consecutive season, the Rockets resisted the temptation to jump into the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes after adding former MVP Durant last summer. General manager Rafael Stone and coach Ime Udoka will instead lean on growth from the team's collection of young talent acquired in recent years, not to mention the continuity that comes with those players developing together over multiple seasons.

Houston signed Tari Eason to a five-year, $81.5 million extension over the summer. But outside of that, the Rockets focused on bolstering depth by bringing aboard veterans Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic. The club also brought in renowned shooting coach Chip Engelland from Oklahoma City. Engelland spent more than a decade with the San Antonio Spurs, winning two titles. -- Wright

San Antonio Spurs: Aug. 10
Key additions: F Tobias Harris

Key retentions: F Harrison Barnes

Key subtractions: None

San Antonio's surprising run to the NBA Finals never obscured its long-term vision for building a sustainable competitor around Victor Wembanyama. Clearly, the Frenchman views the future similarly, considering he signed a 25% max extension worth $252 million instead of the available 30% supermax escalators that would've rocketed the contract to $303 million.

Wembanyama did it to keep San Antonio's talented young core together for as long as possible, with added flexibility to acquire needed supporting players. The Spurs grabbed one of those in free agency in Harris, an experienced, reliable scorer who adds size (6-foot-8, 226 pounds) and physicality on defense while bolstering frontcourt depth in the draft. -- Wright

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Spurs to make late move for Pulisic?
stories.summary: The deadline for the summer window in Europe closes tomorrow, and Tottenham Hotspur are interested in AC Milan winger Christian Pulisic. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
USMNT and AC Milan winger Christian Pulisic is of interest to Tottenham Hotspur, while AC Milan have Manchester United defender Leny Yoro and Barcelona left back Alejandro Balde. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Tottenham Hotspur are interested in AC Milan winger Christian Pulisic, according to TEAMtalk. It is reported that the Premier League side have made an inquiry for the 27-year-old, having identified him as a potential alternative signing to Liverpool winger and Manchester City-linked Cody Gakpo. Spurs are among multiple teams to have checked on the situation of USMNT star Pulisic, who played no part in the 2-0 Serie A win over Venezia on Friday as he continues his return from injury.

- Chelsea have made AS Roma midfielder Manu Koné their priority target to replace Enzo Fernández, says Footmercato. Koné, 25, has been linked with a €40 million exit all summer, but Argentina international Fernández completes a £120 million move to Manchester City before the window shuts, then

- AC Milan have Manchester United defender Leny Yoro and Barcelona left back Alejandro Balde on their shortlist, Tuttosport reports. Yoro, 20 is reportedly among several players being considered by the Rossoneri, who are exploring the market for defenders, with plans to offload Fikayo Tomori and find a long term option at full back. It is reported that a move for 22-year-old Balde would require an offer worth around €50 million.

- Barcelona are monitoring the situation of Internazionale wing back Federico Dimarco, Gazzetta dello Sport reports. The Blaugrana see the 28-year-old as a key starter due to his ability in the attacking third, but aware of growing interest from the LaLiga club, the Nerazzurri are now considering talks to sign him to a new contract extension. Dimarco made 46 appearances across all competitions for Inter last season.

- Chelsea, Aston Villa, and Newcastle are looking at Bayer Leverkusen striker Christian Kofane, Football Insider reports. All three sides are reportedly exploring a swoop to sign the 20-year-old before the transfer window closes on Tuesday, with the Blues viewing him as a high-potential prospect for the future. Kofane began the new Bundesliga campaign with a goal when coming on as a substitute to score in the 3-2 defeat against SV Elversberg on Saturday.

- Liverpool are lining up a €35 million approach for Genk goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, according to the Liverpool Echo. The Reds have identified the 18-year-old as a potential replacement for Giorgi Mamardashvili, who is attracting interest from Nottingham Forest. A move for Brughmans is expected to be difficult, with Real Madrid among multiple clubs in Europe keeping tabs on his situation. The 6-foot-6 stopper has been capped twice by Belgium as a youth international at U19 level. Liverpool have also agreed a deal to sign 18-year-old striker Djylian N'Guessan from Saint Etienne next summer, according to Fabrizio Romano.

ESPN sources
- Fiorentina are set to sign striker Beto from Everton for a fee in the region of £15 million. Beto, 28, is set to have his medical in Florence on Monday and his departure could prompt Everton to move for United States forward Folarin Balogun. Read

- Barcelona are in "very advanced" negotiations with Arsenal over a deal to sign Brazilian striker Gabriel Jesus. Jesus, 29, has just one year to run on his contract with the English champions and has emerged as an option for Barça following their failure to land Julián Álvarez. Read

- Women's Super League (WSL) side Manchester United are finalizing a deal to sign Mexico international Rebeca Bernal from the NWSL's Washington Spirit. According to the source, an announcement is expected at some point ahead of Manchester United's season-opener on Sept. 4. Read

Done deals
- Manchester City have signed Germany international right back Carlotta Wamser from Bayer Leverkusen. Read

- England international striker Ollie Watkins has joined Al Hilal from Aston Villa for around £51 million, the Saudi Pro League club announced. Read

Other rumors
- Manchester United striker Marcus Rashford wants to stay put despite interest from Chelsea, Newcastle and Aston Villa. (Football Insider)

- VfB Stuttgart winger Jamie Leweling, 25, is on the radar of Liverpool, Everton, and Roma over a loan which includes an obligation to be made permanent for €40 million (Patrick Berger)

- Al Ittihad and Al Shabab have shown interest in Al Hilal striker Karim Benzema. (Diario AS)

- Atletico Madrid have made a new approach for Juventus and Canada international striker Jonathan David. The Serie A club see Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee as his potential successor. (Gazzetta dello Sport)

- Valencia are optimistic of securing a deal to sign Liverpool attacking midfielder Harvey Elliott. (Matteo Moretto)

- Juventus are keen to keep hold of midfielder Nico Gonzalez amid interest from Atletico Madrid. (Marca)

- Crystal Palace have agreed a deal to loan defender Honest Ahanor, who is set to complete a €40 million switch from Atalanta to Chelsea. (Di Marzio)

- Newcastle and Sunderland could battle for the signature of Roma winger Matias Soule. (TEAMtalk)

- Aston Villa have been informed that a £25 million offer would be required to land Crystal Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta. (Football Insider)

- Sunderland are discussing a loan move for Tottenham Hotspur defender Kevin Danso. (Telegraph)

- Everton striker Beto is set to complete a €17 million switch to Fiorentina. (Fabrizio Romano)

- Crystal Palace and Fulham are among several teams interested in Eintracht Frankfurt midfielder Hugo Larsson. (TEAMtalk)

stories.headline: What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records
stories.summary: Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is facing 100 drivers in a unique event called Max vs. 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 challengers, starting from the back of the grid.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is taking part in a unique event called Max vs 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 drivers, starting from the back of the grid.

The 28-year-old currently races in F1, the highest tier in motorsport. He is one of the fiercest competitors out there and is known for his aggressive driving style and fearless overtaking.

But if you have never heard of him, or want to learn more, here is everything you need to know.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

Who is Max Verstappen?
Verstappen was born in Belgium to his Dutch father Jos and his Belgian mother Sophie. His father raced in F1 between 1994-2003 and had two podium finishes, while his mother competed in karts. He currently resides in Monaco.

Who does he race for?
Verstappen started racing go-karts when he was just four years old and started to compete in championships at seven.

He then made his way through the ranks winning several world and European titles in 2013. He raced just one season in Formula 3 before skipping Formula 2 and heading straight to Formula 1.

In 2015, he signed for Red Bull junior team Toro Rosso at the age of 17 before he was promoted to Red Bull a year later.

He then went on to become the youngest ever grand prix winner after taking victory at the Spanish Grand Prix and has been at Red Bull ever since, becoming the most successful driver at the team.

He signed a long-term contract back in March 2022 to stay at the Milton Keynes-based team until the end of 2028, and before the Dutch Grand Prix this year he penned a new deal keeping him at the team until 2030.

What has he achieved?
It was clear from the early days that Verstappen was going to be an exceptional racing driver and he's become a phenomenon since with a killer instinct.

He's had 244 race starts in F1 and has been on the top step of the podium 71 times. He's been on the podium 131 times and is just two pole positions away from reaching 50 career poles.

The Dutchman has four world championships which he won back-to-back in a dominant Red Bull era between 2021-2024.

He also has an impressive list of achievements to his name, one being in 2023 where he recorded the most wins [19] and the most podium finishes [21] in a single season. He also recorded 10 consecutive race victories.

When is Max vs 100?
The event is taking place on Sept. 16 and will be streamed live on Disney+.

Why is he racing in Max vs 100?

Verstappen has never been shy of getting his teeth stuck into other forms of motorsport away from Formula 1. He most recently made his debut at the iconic Nürburgring 24 Hours in May, driving a Mercedes-AMG GT3.

This will be a slightly different challenge for the Dutchman, but no doubt one he will enjoy with his competitive nature.

"In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking," Verstappen said. "Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return."

The event is taking place at Silverstone in the U.K. and a circuit has been purpose-built for the occasion. It's set to be the biggest go-kart event in the world.

- Max Verstappen deal: Good news for Red Bull and F1, bad news for the driver market

- Max Verstappen ends F1 speculation by signing new Red Bull contract to 2030

How is his 2026 F1 season going?
The 2026 season is one with big regulation and rules changes and Red Bull are currently at the back of the front running teams, but are ahead of the midfield pack.

Verstappen is still searching for his first race win of the season, but has been on the podium four times.

He's currently sixth in the title championship and is 130 points adrift from title leader Kimi Antonelli.

stories.headline: Shepard has 22nd double-double this season, Wings beat Sun 97-71
stories.summary: — Arike Ogunbowale scored 18 points, Jessica Shepard had 17 points and 10 rebounds, and the Dallas Wings beat the Connecticut Sun 97-71 on Sunday night in the final game before the FIBA World Cup break.
stories.body:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- — Arike Ogunbowale scored 18 points, Jessica Shepard had 17 points and 10 rebounds, and the Dallas Wings beat the Connecticut Sun 97-71 on Sunday night in the final game before the FIBA World Cup break.


The Wings (24-16) have won four in a row and have their most wins in a season since 2007, when the franchise also won 24 games as the Detroit Shock. The Shock won a franchise-record 25 games in 2003 on their way to the first of three WNBA championships.


Dallas moved into a three-way tie with New York and Washington for sixth in the WNBA standings, two games back of Indiana and Atlanta.


Shepard had her 22nd double-double this season, second most in the WNBA — after Angel Reese with 29 — to extend the franchise record. Paige Bueckers added 15 points and six assists and Maddy Siegrist scored 11 for Dallas.


Aaliyah Edwards scored 21 of her career-best tying 26 points in the first half for the Sun (10-30). Charlisse Leger-Walker hit five 3-pointers and finished with 17 points.


Saniya Rivers made a driving layup that gave the Sun their first lead about 4 1/2 minutes into the game at 11-10, but Bueckers scored inside 11 seconds later to put Dallas back in front for good.


Connecticut, which trailed by 13 at halftime, made 4 of 17 (23.5%) from the field, 1 of 6 from behind the arc, and hit 3 of 6 from the free-throw line as it was outscored 23-12 in the third quarter.


Up next
Sun: Plays Sept. 17 at Atlanta.


Wings: Host Los Angeles on Sept. 17.


----


This story has been updated to correct that the Shock won 24 games in 2007, not 24 straight.

stories.body:
Record 15-time European champions Real Madrid will start the league phase of the Champions League on Sept. 8 when they host coach José Mourinho's former club Inter Milan.

Match dates for each of the 36 teams' eight-game schedules were published Saturday by UEFA, two days after the draw in Monaco.

- Champions League draw: Good for Liverpool, bad for Barcelona

- Arsenal-Madrid, PSG-Barça highlight UCL draw

- Champions League draw becomes UEFA's latest stand against FIFA president Infantino

In two early starts on the opening day, Club Brugge will host Aston Villa and AEK Athens will welcome LASK, the newcomers from Austria. Both games will kick off at 6:45 p.m.

One day later, defending champions Paris Saint-Germain will host Slovan Bratislava -- coached by Yaya Touré, the first African leading a team at the league phase -- and Liverpool will host Atlético Madrid, a repeat of their opening game last season. That was a 3-2 win for Liverpool at Anfield.

Debut-making Sabah of Azerbaijan will start at Manchester United on Sept. 10, the same day Como host RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich welcome Bodo/Glimt.

Tough October for PSG
Manchester City hosting PSG on Oct. 14 is a highlight of the second round of games played more than one month later, after the new and extended four-game slate for national teams.

PSG will then face Barcelona at Parc des Princes on Oct. 20, one day before Bayern Munich host Arsenal.

Barcelona's next trip will then be a long way east to play Sabah in Baku on Nov. 25, before the Spanish champions hosts Man City on Dec. 8.

Arsenal will host Real Madrid on Dec. 9 for the first of coach Mourinho's scheduled two visits to London.

Madrid will return on the final match day, Jan. 27, to face Shakhtar Donetsk at Chelsea, where Mourinho won three Premier League titles for the club's Russian then-owner Roman Abramovich. Stamford Bridge is the Ukrainian champions' choice of neutral venue for its four home games.

Welcome to Norway
The two Norwegian teams each must have a home game in January, during their domestic offseason when the weather should be most severe, and both will be in the seventh round.

Bodo/Glimt will welcome Atlético Madrid to the Arctic Circle at their tiny stadium on Jan. 19 and Viking will host PSV Eindhoven in Stavanger one day later.

Final round
The final round on Jan. 27 sees all 18 games start at the same time, when it's 9 p.m. in central Europe, and Barcelona will host newcomers Como coached by their former star Cesc Fàbregas.

Como get the toughest January run-in after hosting PSG one week earlier.

PSG will finish by hosting Galatasaray, Arsenal will host Sabah and Bayern will host Real Betis.

The top eight teams in the final standings go directly to the round of 16 in March. Teams placed ninth to 24th enter the knockout playoffs in February to decide the other eight teams in the round of 16. Teams placed 25th to 36th are eliminated.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Song Yadong KO's Umar Nurmagomedov in massive UFC upset
stories.summary: Song Yadong pulled off a massive upset by knocking out heavily favored Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night in Shanghai.
stories.body:
Song Yadong saved the greatest performance of his career for his home country, knocking out former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night on Saturday in Shanghai.

Song (24-9-1, 1 NC), a nearly 5-1 underdog at DraftKings Sportsbook, dropped Nurmagomedov with a short right hand, drawing a roar from the crowd when the fight was waved off at 1 minute, 48 seconds of Round 2.

"I believe in myself, and my team believed that I would win this fight," Song said through an interpreter. "They told me I would knock this guy out, and I did it."

It was the second straight fight in China for Song and his second straight win by finish. His most recent knockout win had been in 2023.

Song, making his first appearance in Shanghai since his UFC debut at age 19 in 2017, walked out to a hero's welcome.

"Nine years ago, I wanted to show I could walk in this Octagon," he said. "Nine years later, I want to prove I am the best in the world. I am the best Chinese fighter in the world."

The knockout came after Nurmagomedov (20-2) ducked out of the way of a left hand and right into the path of a short right hand, which connected near his right ear and sent him limply to the canvas. Song delivered three finishing shots on the mat before the referee jumped in.

That sent Song running around inside the cage in celebration, where he nearly ran into Nurmagomedov's younger brother and cornerman, PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov, who had rushed in to check on his fallen brother. Usman Nurmagomedov appeared to throw an elbow in Song's direction as the elated winner was running past.

Song climbed atop the cage to soak in the fans' cheers before jumping down outside the cage and running into the crowd to get hugs and high-fives from fans.

"Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, maybe not next month, but I will be the first male Chinese UFC champion," Song said through the interpreter, with the "male" designation a nod to countrywoman Zhang Weili, a two-time women's champion at strawweight.

Song, who trains in Sacramento, California, switched to English and yelled, "Give me the title shot!"

stories.headline: Avalanche's Makar agrees to record deal worth $20.4M annually
stories.summary: Cale Makar has agreed to an eight-year extension with the Avalanche that will make him the highest-paid player in NHL history with a $20.4 million average annual value.
stories.body:
Cale Makar has agreed to an eight-year extension with the Colorado Avalanche that will make him the highest-paid player in NHL history.

The deal carries a $20.4 million average annual value. Makar is the first player in league history to make at least $20 million per season. The max a player could make, per percentage of the salary cap, is $20.8 million.

Makar, 27, has been a finalist for the Norris Trophy as the league's top defenseman for six consecutive seasons. He is one of only 14 players to win multiple Norris Trophies, winning the award twice -- most recently in 2025.

Makar was entering the final year of his contract, which carried a $9 million average annual value.

The deal carries a full no-movement clause, according to sources. The eight-year term carries significance because when the new collective bargaining rules kick in Sept. 15, players will be able to sign for a maximum of only seven years.

This summer has seen record-breaking contracts in the NHL thanks to a rising salary cap, including massive deals for young centers Macklin Celebrini and Leo Carlsson.

Makar is a centerpiece for the Avalanche, perennial Stanley Cup contenders who won the Presidents' Trophy last season.

stories.headline: Knights prop ruled out of NRL finals with mammoth ban
stories.summary: Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.
stories.body:
Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.

Saifiti was sent off in the first half of Sunday's 46-32 defeat in Auckland and was handed a grade two reckless high tackle charge by the NRL's match review committee on Monday morning.

The Knights are on the bye for the final round of the regular season, meaning Saifiti's ban will only kick in for their first finals game.

Newcastle - currently sitting seventh - will play an elimination final in week one but even if they were to upset the odds and qualify for the grand final, the Fijian prop would still be on the sidelines with suspension.

Saifiti's only hope of playing in the NRL again this season hinge on the prop contesting the charge at the judiciary on Tuesday in a bid to reduce his punishment.

Should the front-rower fight the suspension and lose his appeal, he will have another week added to his four-game ban.

Elsewhere, Cronulla prop Tom Hazelton is set to miss Cronulla's final regular season game against Melbourne after being cited for a hip-drop tackle on Ronald Volkman.

Hazelton was sin-binned by referee Ashley Klein late in Sunday's loss to Parramatta but will serve a one-game ban with an early guilty plea and be free to return for week one of the final series.
